children.translated_text: There he states the primacy of substance with the words, "substance itself."
Among taste and the other factors, substance alone is primary.

children.text: hi yasmāt te rasādayaḥ tadāśrayāḥ dravyādhiṣṭhānāḥ ||
children.translated_text: For those, taste and the rest, have that as their support; they are founded upon substance.
By this very statement it is said that substance is the support of taste and the other qualities.
The statement of primacy is intended to make knowledge of substance the main point.
And it is said in the <s>Saṃgraha</s>:
Since barley is seen to be sweet and heavy, yet it increases wind,
and ghee, though cold, kindles digestion, while fat, though hot, depresses the digestive fire;
mung bean, though pungent in post-digestive effect, allays bile, while black gram is bilious;
and molasses, though sweet in post-digestive effect, causes accumulation, being unctuous, hot, and heavy;

children.text: rase svādau yathā caitat tathānyeṣvapi dṛśyate
children.translated_text: as this is so in the case of sweet taste, so it is seen also in the other tastes.
The fruit of the <s>ākṣakī</s>, though sour, is windy and destroys phlegm and bile.

children.text: kurute dadhi gurveva vahniṃ pārevataṃ na tu
children.translated_text: Curds, being heavy, do kindle the digestive fire, but the pigeon does not.
The wood-apple and pomegranate are sour and constipating, but the emblic myrobalan fruit is not.

children.text: kaṣāyā grāhiṇī śītā dhātakī na harītakī
children.translated_text: <s>Dhātakī</s> is astringent, constipating, and cold, but <s>harītakī</s> is not.
Therefore taste and the other factors are not primary separately; rather, they are dependent.

children.text: prabhāvaśca yato dravye dravyaṃ śreṣṭham ato matam
children.translated_text: And since special efficacy also resides in substance, substance is therefore held to be superior.
Thus.
He states the divisions of substance with the words, "made of the five elements."

children.text: pañca saṃkhyākāni bhūtānyeva ātmāno yasya tattathā pārthivādibhedāt pañcadhetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That whose very selves are the five elements in number is such; the meaning is that it is fivefold by the divisions beginning with earth.
Because cause and effect are figuratively treated as non-different, the word "element" denotes what is elemental, that is, materially composed.
The word "substance" is carried forward.
He states the origination of substance with the words, "but that."

children.text: tat dravyam kṣmāṃ pṛthivīm adhiṣṭhāya jāyate mṛdam iva ghaṭaḥ upādānakāraṇam pṛthvītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That substance arises by resting on earth, the ground, just as a pot arises from clay; the meaning is that earth is the material cause.

children.text: ambu udakaṃ yoniḥ vipariṇāmakāraṇaṃ yasya tadambuyoni ||
children.translated_text: Water is the womb, the cause of transformation, of that substance; therefore it is water-born.
This is as, in the production of a pot, clay becomes compacted and so on.
Its completion, its having all its parts, occurs through connection with fire and the other elements, by their giving hardness, activity, space, and so forth.
The mutual distinction too comes from that very source.
For example, from clay that has been made into a lump arise distinctions such as jewel, cup, and dish.

children.text: sarveṣām pañcabhūtātmakatvādabhede prāpte bhedahetumāha vyapadeśa iti ||
children.translated_text: Since, because all things are made of the five elements, non-difference would follow, he states the cause of distinction with the word "designation."

children.text: vyapadeśaḥ idaṃ pārthivamidamāpyam ityādi bhedena vyavahāraḥ ||
children.translated_text: Designation is practical usage by distinction, such as "this is earthy" and "this is watery."

children.text: sa bhūyasā adhikena bhūtena yatra yasyādhikyaṃ tasya tena vyapadeśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: It is made according to the element that is greater: wherever there is predominance of a given element, designation is made by that element.
He states that all substances possess all properties with the word "therefore."

children.text: tasmāt sarvabhūtārabdhatvāt sarvamapi dravyaṃ naikarasam anekarasam sarvadharmam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because everything is begun from all the elements, every substance is not of one taste but of many tastes; that is, it has all properties.
Here the word "taste" indicates any property whatsoever.

children.text: sarvabhūtārabdhatve 'pyekarasatve ko doṣaḥ ityāśaṅkyāha bhūtasaṃghātasambhavād iti ||
children.translated_text: Anticipating the objection, "Even if it is begun from all elements, what fault is there if it has only one taste?" he says, "because it is produced from an aggregate of elements."
For even tastes arise from a collection of elements.

children.text: vakṣyati hi dvayolbaṇaiḥ kramād bhūtair madhurādirasodbhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For he will say, "The sweet and other tastes arise in order from two predominant elements."
Thus.
And when the cause exists, the effect must necessarily come to be.

children.text: tulyanyāyatvaprasaṅgāt sarveṣāṃ rogāṇāṃ sarvadoṣajatvam āha naikadoṣā iti ||
children.translated_text: Because the same reasoning would apply, he states that all diseases are produced by all the doṣas with the words, "not of one doṣa."
Diseases are not of one doṣa; all diseases arise from all the doṣas.

children.text: kutaḥ tata eva hetoḥ rogāṇāmapi bhūtasaṃghātasambhavāt ||
children.translated_text: Why? For that very reason: diseases too arise from an aggregate of elements.
And the aggregate of elements is divided among the three doṣas.
As is said in the <s>Saṃgraha</s>:

children.text: vāyvākāśadhātubhyāṃ vāyuḥ āgneyaṃ pittam ambhaḥpṛthivībhyāṃ śleṣmā ||
children.translated_text: From the air and space elements comes wind; bile is fiery; phlegm comes from water and earth.
Thus.

children.text: bhūtasaṃghātaṃ vinā na doṣasaṃghātaḥ taṃ vinā na rogotpattir iti ataḥ sarve rogāstridoṣajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Without an aggregate of elements there is no aggregate of doṣas; without that there is no arising of disease. Therefore all diseases are born of the three doṣas.

children.text: kecit tu sarvadravyāṇāṃ sarvarasatvena sarvadoṣasāmānyāt sarvadoṣakopanatvam tato rogā naikadoṣā iti vyācakṣate ||
children.translated_text: Some, however, explain "diseases are not of one doṣa" as follows: because all substances have all tastes, they have common relation to all doṣas and therefore provoke all doṣas.
That is incorrect.
For opposition also exists, just as commonality does.
If one says that commonality is the operative factor, no, because it would follow that there are no distinct substances that remove doṣas.

children.text: vaiparītyamapi kvacit prayojakam iti cen na sarvadoṣakopanatvaniyamavyāghātāt ||
children.translated_text: If one says that opposition too is sometimes operative, no, because that contradicts the rule that all substances provoke all doṣas.

children.text: sarvadoṣakopanānāṃ niyama iti cen na dvyekadoṣakopanadravyābhāvaprasaṅgāt ||
children.translated_text: If one says there is a rule among things that provoke all doṣas, no, because it would follow that there are no substances that provoke two doṣas or one doṣa.
If one says that designation is made in this way merely by predominance, no, because it would follow that there are no substances that provoke two doṣas and calm one, or calm two and provoke one.

children.text: siddhānte'pi sarveṣāṃ sarvadharmatvasvīkārānna doṣaghnādivibhāga iti cet na tasya tasya dharmasya tatra tatra prayojakatvāt ||
children.translated_text: If one objects that even in the established doctrine, since all things are accepted as possessing all properties, there can be no division such as doṣa-removing substances, no, because each particular property is operative in each particular case.
And accordingly he will say:

children.text: kiṃcid rasena kurute karma pākena cāparam
children.translated_text: Something performs an action by its taste, and another action by its post-digestive effect;
something by another quality, by potency, or indeed by special efficacy.
And so on.
Therefore the earlier explanation is correct.

children.text: sarveṣāṃ sarvadharmatvādaviśeṣe prāpte tannirāsārthaṃ dharmatāratamyam āha tatra vyakta iti ||
children.translated_text: Since, because all things possess all properties, lack of distinction would follow, he states the gradation among properties in order to remove that with the words, "among them, manifest."

children.text: tatra dravye kaściddharmaḥ sadyo vyaktaḥ kaścidavyaktaḥ kaścid īṣad vyaktaḥ kaścidante vyaktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In a substance, one property is immediately manifest, another is unmanifest, another is slightly manifest, and another is manifest at the end.
Among these, the first is called taste; the other three are called secondary tastes.

children.text: gurvādīnāṃ rasāśrayatvād dravyasyāsarvadharmatve prāpte parihāram āha gurvādaya iti ||
children.translated_text: Since, because heaviness and the other qualities depend on taste, it would follow that substance does not possess all properties, he states the answer with the words, "heaviness and the rest."

children.text: gurvādayo guṇā dravya eva na raseṣu ||
children.translated_text: The qualities beginning with heaviness belong to substance itself, not to the tastes.

children.text: yastu madhuro guruḥ amlo laghurityādi vyapadeśaḥ sa sāhacaryopacārataḥ ||
children.translated_text: But expressions such as 'the sweet is heavy' and 'the sour is light' are based on figurative usage arising from association.
Association is the presence of two things in one substrate.
In answer to the question, 'How is there association at all?', he says, 'as the substrate of taste.'
For substance is the substrate of the tastes, just as it is of heaviness and the other qualities.

children.text: ata ekāśrayatvāt sāhacaryam tena upacāraḥ avidyamānasyāpy āśrayāśrayībhāvasyāropaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because they have one substrate, there is association; through that there is figurative usage, namely the superimposition of a relation of substrate and supported thing even where it does not really exist.

children.text: nanu kimetat rasādvyatiriktaṃ dravyaṃ nāma ityata āha pṛthivyādāv iti ||
children.translated_text: Now, in response to the objection, 'What is this substance, distinct from taste, called?', he says, 'in earth and so on.'
The meaning is: substance is what is denoted by words such as earth.
Next he defines the divisions of substance.
There he defines the earthy substance with the words 'there, substance.'
An earthy substance is one in which qualities such as heaviness are predominant and which causes heaviness and the like.
Compactness means hardness.
Increase means stoutness; the word 'quality' here denotes a property.
The word 'predominant' is used because all properties belong to all substances.
He defines the watery substance with 'liquid and cold.'
A watery substance is a substance in which qualities such as liquidity are predominant and which causes oleation and the like.
Although liquid and dense are mutually opposed, they are watery because of their common character of moistness.
Oozing is the flowing of channels; refreshment is satisfaction.
He defines the fiery substance with 'dry and sharp.'
A fiery substance is a substance in which qualities such as dryness are predominant and which causes burning and the like.
Radiance is brilliance.
Color is such as whiteness and the like.
Illumination is light.
Cooking is digestion or maturation.
Its being of that nature is said by figuratively treating effect and cause as non-different.
He defines the airy substance with 'airy.'
An airy substance is a substance in which qualities such as dryness are predominant and which causes dryness and the like.
Movement is activity of various kinds.
He defines the etheric substance with 'etheric.'
An etheric substance is a substance in which qualities such as subtlety are predominant and which causes porosity and the like.
Porosity means being full of openings.
He states that substance as such has medicinal character with the word 'in the world.'

children.text: evam uktena prakāreṇa tasya tasya dravyasya tattadguṇayogatvāt jagati na kiṃcid dravyamanauṣadhaṃ vidyate sarvameva dravyam auṣadham ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the manner stated, because each substance is connected with its respective qualities, there is no substance in the world that is not a medicine; every substance is indeed a medicine.

children.text: kutaḥ nānārthayogayor vaśād arthaḥ prayojanam yogo yojanā nānāvidhāv arthayogau nānārthayogau tayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: Why? Because of its connection with various purposes: purpose is use, and yoga is application; various purposes and applications are 'various-purpose-applications,' and because of them.

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati yadekasminnarthe nopayujyate tad evānyasminn upayujyate ||
children.translated_text: What is being said is this: that which is not useful for one purpose is useful for another.
That which is not useful through one application is useful through another application.

children.text: yathā atyantānupayukto'pi kharameṣādiviḍraso binduśaḥ śvāsakāsādau atyantāpathyo'pi māṣa iṇḍurīkṛtaḥ sanavanīto 'rditādau ||
children.translated_text: For example, the juice of the dung of donkeys, sheep, and the like, though utterly useless, is useful drop by drop in dyspnea, cough, and so on; and black gram, though extremely unwholesome, when made into iṇḍurī and mixed with fresh butter, is useful in facial paralysis and the like.

children.text: auṣadhadvaividhyaṃ pañcavidhe dravye vibhajati dravyam ūrdhvagamam iti ||
children.translated_text: He divides the twofold medicine among the fivefold substances with 'substance goes upward.'

children.text: dvividhamauṣadham śodhanaṃ śamanaṃ ca śodhanaṃ dvividham ūrdhvagamam adhogamaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Medicine is of two kinds: purifying and pacifying. Purification is of two kinds, upward-moving and downward-moving.
There, that in which fire and wind are predominant is upward-moving; that which has the qualities of earth and water is downward-moving.
By elimination, that in which ether is predominant is pacifying.

children.text: tathā ca suśrutaḥ ākāśaguṇabhūyiṣṭhaṃ saṃśamanam iti ||
children.translated_text: And so <s>Suśruta</s> says: 'That in which the quality of ether is most abundant is pacifying.'
Going is motion.
That whose motion is upward is upward-moving.
The words 'generally' and 'most abundant' are meant to allow exceptions.

children.text: yathā citrakavad agnipavanotkaṭāyā api dantyā virecanatvam mṛdvīkāvad bhūmitoyaguṇādhikasyāpi madhukasya vamanatvam ||
children.translated_text: For example, dantī, though predominant in fire and wind, is purgative like citraka; and madhuka, though rich in the qualities of earth and water, is emetic like grapes.
But in the compendium, what has a mixed nature works in both directions.
Pacifying, however, was stated earlier as possessing qualities opposite to the doṣa.
And when there is a mixture of those, the decision is made according to predominance.

children.text: tatsaṃkare guṇasaṃkare yato bāhulyena yeṣāṃ guṇānāṃ bāhulyaṃ tair nirṇayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When those are mixed, that is, when the qualities are mixed, the determination is made by whatever is predominant, namely by those qualities whose abundance is greater.
Similarly, what is of the nature of wind is absorbent.
What is of the nature of fire kindles appetite and digests.
What is of both natures scrapes or reduces.
What is of the nature of earth and water nourishes.
Thus.
He concludes the subject matter of the section with 'thus, substance.'
The word 'thus' marks completion.

children.text: kramaprāptasya rasasyānabhidhāne hetumāha raso bhedair iti ||
children.translated_text: Since taste comes next in order but is not being discussed here, he gives the reason with 'taste, by its divisions.'

children.text: uttaratra uttarasminnadhyāye upadekṣyate vakṣyate yato'sau bahubhirbhedairviśiṣṭaḥ bahubhedatvena bahuvaktavyatvāt pṛthagadhyāyakaraṇamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: It will be taught, that is, stated later in the following chapter, because it is distinguished by many divisions; the meaning is that a separate chapter is made because, on account of having many divisions, much must be said about it.
Now, potency.
There he presents the view of others with 'potency, again.'

children.text: eke khāraṇādiprabhṛtayaḥ gurvādīn guṇān vīryaṃ ca vadanti ||
children.translated_text: Some, beginning with Khāraṇa and others, say that the qualities beginning with heaviness are also potency.
And in this way it is accepted as eightfold.

children.text: suśrutastu gurulaghū vihāya viśadapicchilau paṭhati kecid aṣṭavidham āhur uṣṇaṃ śītaṃ snigdhaṃ rūkṣaṃ viśadaṃ picchilaṃ mṛdu tīkṣṇaṃ ceti ||
children.translated_text: But <s>Suśruta</s>, leaving aside heavy and light, reads clear and slimy: some say it is eightfold, namely hot, cold, unctuous, dry, clear, slimy, soft, and sharp.
Thus.
He presents <s>Caraka</s>'s view with 'but <s>Caraka</s> says.'

children.text: yena kriyate tad vīryam dravyakartṛke karmaṇi karaṇabhūtam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That by which an action is performed is potency; the meaning is that, in an action whose agent is a substance, it is the instrumental cause.
When it is expected, 'Of how many kinds is that?', he says, 'whatever action.'

children.text: yā kriyā yena kriyate tasyāṃ tadvīryam yāvatyaḥ kriyās tāvantyeva vīryāṇītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whatever action is performed by whatever thing, that thing is the potency in that action; the meaning is that there are exactly as many potencies as there are actions.
Why? He says, 'not without potency.'

children.text: avīryaṃ dravyaṃ na kiṃcit kurute vīryaṃ vinā kartṛtvaṃ nāstītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A substance without potency does nothing; the meaning is that without potency there is no agency.

children.text: kutaḥ ityāha sarvā vīryakṛtā hi sā ||
children.translated_text: Why? He says, 'For all of that is produced by potency.'

children.text: hi yasmāt sā kriyā sarvāpi vīryakṛtā ||
children.translated_text: For, since that action, all of it, is produced by potency.

children.text: nanu evaṃ rasādīnāmapi vīryatvaprasaṅga ityāha gurvādiṣviti ||
children.translated_text: But, if so, there would also be the consequence that taste and the others are potencies. To this he says, 'among heaviness and the rest.'

children.text: tena carakeṇa gurvādiṣv eva vīryākhyā varṇyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore <s>Caraka</s> describes the name 'potency' only among heaviness and the other such qualities.
Why? Because it is etymologically appropriate.
The word 'iti' has the sense of a reason.
Because, when the term 'potency' is applied to them, it would be etymologically appropriate.
He shows precisely this etymological appropriateness with 'complete' and the following words.
For potency is an instrument.
And an instrument is what is most effective in accomplishing something.
And the status of being most effective belongs only to heaviness and the rest.
Why? Because they are the essence of the complete set of qualities.

children.text: samagreṣu guṇeṣu madhye sthiratvāc cirasthāyitvāt śaktyutkarṣavivartanāt utkṛṣṭaśaktitvāt vyavahārāya mukhyatvāt loke śāstre ca mukhyatvena vyavahriyamāṇatvāt bahvagragrahaṇād bahuguṇagaṇanāyāṃ prathamagrahaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: Among all the qualities, because of stability, that is, long duration; because of the manifestation of superior power, that is, possessing eminent power; because of primacy for practical usage, that is, being treated as primary both in the world and in śāstra; and because of being taken first among many, that is, being mentioned first in the enumeration of many qualities.

children.text: vipāke'pi sthiratvasya prabhāve'pi śaktyutkarṣasya mṛdukaṭhinādāv api vyavahāramukhyatvasya raseṣv api bahvagragrahaṇasya darśanāt caturṇām upādānam ||
children.translated_text: Because stability is also seen in <s>vipāka</s>, superior power also in special effect, primacy in usage also in softness, hardness, and the like, and being taken first among many also among tastes, the four reasons are adopted.

children.text: etac ca rasādiṣu nāstīti darśayati ataś ceti ||
children.translated_text: And he shows that this is not present in taste and the rest with 'and therefore.'

children.text: sā vīryākhyā rasādiṣu sambhavatyapi vidyamānāpi na vivakṣyate anudarā kanyetivat ||
children.translated_text: That name 'potency,' though possible and though present among taste and the rest, is not intended there, as in the expression 'a girl without a belly.'

children.text: kriyānirvartanasāmānyāt satyapi vīryatve rasādayo vīryatvena na vyavahriyanta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that although taste and the rest really have the nature of potency because they share in bringing about action, they are not conventionally spoken of as potency.
Why? Because they are the opposite of those four reasons.
He rejects the already established sense with 'potency.'

children.text: hi sphuṭam ataḥ kāraṇāt gurvādaya eva vīryam ||
children.translated_text: For, clearly, for this reason, heaviness and the rest alone are potency.
The sense is that the name 'potency' is conventionally fixed for the eight qualities beginning with heaviness.
Because he is not satisfied with the previous opinion, he presents another opinion with 'hot and cold.'

children.text: anye suśrutādayaḥ uṣṇaṃ śītaṃ ceti dvividham eva vīryam ācakṣate vadanti ||
children.translated_text: Others, beginning with <s>Suśruta</s>, say that potency is only twofold: hot and cold.

children.text: uktamatasyopapattim āha api ceti nānātmakam iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the justification of the opinion just mentioned with 'moreover' and 'of manifold nature.'

children.text: na kevalaṃ matamātram idam yuktaṃ cedaṃ pūrvasmān matāt ityapi cety asyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This is not merely an opinion; rather, this is also more reasonable than the previous opinion. That is the meaning of 'moreover.'

children.text: nānātmakamapi pṛthivyādyanekakaraṇam api dravyamagnīṣomau jātucitkadācidapi nātikrāmati tayor vaśe vartate kiṃcid āgneyatvād uṣṇaṃ kiṃcit saumyatvācchītam iti dvidhaiva gatir ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A substance, even though of manifold nature, that is, even though having many causes such as earth and the rest, never at any time transgresses fire and soma; it remains under their control. Some substance is hot because it is fiery, and some is cold because it is somatic. Thus its course is only twofold.
Why? Because those two are very powerful.
For this very reason, heaviness and the other qualities overpower all qualities.
And hot and cold overpower even heaviness and the rest.

children.text: atra dṛṣṭāntam āha yathā viśvaṃ kartṛ vyaktāvyaktākhyabhedadvayaṃ nātikrāmati ||
children.translated_text: Here he gives an example: just as the whole universe, the agent, does not transgress the twofold division called manifest and unmanifest.
He defines the hot with 'there.'
That which produces dizziness and the like is of hot potency.
Quick cooking means rapid digestion or maturation.
He defines the cold with 'cool' and 'refreshment.'
That which produces refreshment and the like is of cold potency.
Refreshment is relief.
Life-sustaining is the support of life through removal of fainting and the like.
Checking is the removal of sweat.
The clarity of blood and bile is their purity.
Now, <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect).
There he defines <s>vipāka</s> with 'by the gastric.'

children.text: rasānāṃ rasavatāṃ dravyāṇāṃ jāṭharāgninā saṃyogād yadrasāntaram utpadyate sa vipākaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The other taste that arises from the conjunction of tastes, that is, of substances possessing taste, with the gastric fire is <s>vipāka</s>.
At first, even food of six tastes may be said to have become sweet.

children.text: ityādyuktānāṃ madhurāmlakaṭupākānāṃ vyāvṛttyartham āha pariṇāmānte āhārapariṇāmānte ||
children.translated_text: To exclude the sweet, sour, and pungent stages of digestion taught in such passages, he says 'at the end of transformation,' that is, at the end of the transformation of food.

children.text: te tu pariṇāmātprāgeva utpadyante iti teṣāṃ rasatvam eva ||
children.translated_text: But those arise before the completion of transformation, and therefore they are only tastes.
He states the threefold nature of <s>vipāka</s> with 'sweet.'

children.text: svāduḥ paṭuś ca madhuro lavaṇaśca madhuraṃ pacyate pakvo madhuratvaṃ yātītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sweet and sharp, and sweet and salty, are digested into sweetness; the meaning is that, when cooked, they attain sweetness.
'Sweetly' is an adverb qualifying the action.
'Is digested' is an ātmanepada form in the passive-agent construction.
In the same way, a sour taste is digested into sourness.
For the three beginning with bitter, the <s>vipāka</s> is pungent.

children.text: madhurarasasyāpi vrīhervipāke'mlatvāt lavaṇasyāpi sauvarcalasya kaṭuvipākatvāt amlatiktoṣaṇānām api dāḍimapaṭolapippalīnāṃ madhuratvāt kaṣāyasyāpi kulatthasyāmlavipākatvāt prāyaśa ityuktam matāntarasaṃgrahārthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Because rice, though sweet in taste, has sourness in <s>vipāka</s>; sauvarcala salt, though salty, has pungent <s>vipāka</s>; pomegranate, paṭola, and long pepper, though sour, bitter, and pungent, have sweetness; and horse gram, though astringent, has sour <s>vipāka</s>, the word 'generally' is used, and also in order to include another opinion.

children.text: tatra dvau vipākāv iti suśrutaḥ dravyeṣu pacyamāneṣu yeṣv ambupṛthivīguṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In that regard <s>Suśruta</s> says that there are two <s>vipākas</s>: 'When substances are being digested, those in which the qualities of water and earth
become predominant: in such cases the digestive result is considered sweet.
But in those substances being digested in which the qualities of fire, wind, and ether
become predominant: in such cases the digestive result is considered pungent.'
Thus.

children.text: parāśarastu tiktakaṣāyayor madhuravipākam āha pākāstrayo rasānām amlo 'mlaṃ pacyate kaṭuḥ kaṭukam
children.translated_text: But <s>Parāśara</s> states that bitter and astringent have sweet <s>vipāka</s>: 'There are three digestive results of tastes. Sour is digested into sour, pungent into pungent,
and the other four into sweet; but mixed tastes are digested into a mixed result.'

children.text: kaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇāṃ kaṭuko yeṣāṃ vipāka iti pakṣaḥ
children.translated_text: There is also the view: 'Those for which the <s>vipāka</s> of pungent, bitter, and astringent is pungent,
how can bitter and astringent exist when their pitta has been obstructed?'
Thus.

children.text: ṣoḍhā pākastu saṃgrahe nirastaḥ yathārasaṃ jaguḥ pākān ṣaṭ kecit tad asāṃpratam
children.translated_text: The sixfold digestion is rejected in the Saṃgraha: some have stated six digestions according to each taste, but that is not acceptable.

children.text: yatsvādur vrīhir amlatvaṃ na cāmlamapi dāḍimam ||
children.translated_text: For rice, which is sweet, comes to sourness, while the pomegranate, though sour, does not become sour in digestion.

children.text: yāti tailaṃ ca kaṭutāṃ kaṭukāpi na pippalī
children.translated_text: And oil comes to pungency, while long pepper, though pungent, does not.
If digestions corresponded to the tastes, such an inversion would not occur.
Thus.

children.text: trayāṇāṃ pākānāṃ lakṣaṇam āha rasair iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the definition of the three digestions with 'by the tastes.'

children.text: asau trividho vipākaḥ yathāsvaṃ rasair madhurāmlakaṭukaiḥ tulyaphalaḥ tulyakāryo jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This threefold <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect) should be understood as having effects equivalent to its respective sweet, sour, and pungent tastes, that is, as having the same action.

children.text: madhurasya rasasya kāryaṃ dṛṣṭvā madhuraḥ pāko lakṣaṇīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Having observed the action of the sweet taste, the sweet digestion is to be characterized.
Likewise, from the sour taste the sour digestion, and from the pungent taste the pungent one.

children.text: dravyādīnāṃ pṛthak prayojakatvamāha tatra dravyam iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the separate causal efficacy of substance and the others with 'there, substance.'
By another quality, that is, by a quality distinct from taste, such as heaviness and the like.
This very point also makes known that taste and the others too have the character of qualities.

children.text: tena palāṇḍus taduṣṇair nyūnaḥ ityādiprayogā upapannāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore usages such as 'onion is inferior to that because of its heat' and the like are justified.
By special effect, that is, by its own nature itself.
The special effect of a substance is its own inherent power.

children.text: tathā ca suśrutaḥ tad dravyamātmanā kiṃcit kiṃcid vīryeṇa sevitam
children.translated_text: And so <s>Suśruta</s> says: that substance, when used, does something by its own nature, something by potency,

children.text: kiṃcid rasavipākābhyāṃ doṣaṃ hanti karoti ca ||
children.translated_text: and something by taste and digestion; it destroys and also produces a <s>doṣa</s>.
Thus.
A beneficial action is the pacification of a <s>doṣa</s>; a harmful one is the aggravation of a <s>doṣa</s>.
'Something,' 'another thing,' and 'some thing' are three qualifiers of agent and action.

children.text: yadā bahūni dravyāṇi ekameva karma kurvanti tadā kartṛviśeṣaṇam yadaikam eva dravyaṃ bahūni karmāṇi tadā karmaviśeṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: When many substances perform just one action, it is a qualifier of the agent; when one substance performs many actions, it is a qualifier of the action.

children.text: etaccodāhṛtaṃ saṃgrahe tatra yanmadhuraṃ rasavipākayoḥ śītavīryaṃ ca dravyaṃ yaccāmlaṃ tayoruṣṇavīryaṃ ca yadvā kaṭukaṃ teṣāṃ yathāsvaṃ rasādibhyaḥ prāyo guṇān doṣakopanaśamanatvaṃ ca vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: And this has been illustrated in the Saṃgraha: there, a substance that is sweet in taste and digestion and also cold in potency, one that is sour in both and also hot in potency, or one that is pungent, should generally be known from its respective taste and so on as having qualities and as aggravating or pacifying <s>doṣas</s>.
For example, milk, wine, black pepper, and the like.
But when taste and the others are mixed, the result is otherwise.

children.text: yathā madhu madhuraṃ śleṣmāṇaṃ śamayati kaṭuvipākitayā sakaṣāyatvād raukṣyācca vātaṃ janayati śītavīryatvāc ca ||
children.translated_text: For example, honey, though sweet, pacifies phlegm because it has pungent digestion, and it produces wind because it is somewhat astringent and dry, and also because it has cold potency.
So too barley.
The flesh of marsh and aquatic animals, though cold, produces bile because it has hot potency.

children.text: tathā tailaṃ kaṭuvipākitayā ca vipākata eva baddhaviṇmūtram ||
children.translated_text: Likewise oil, because it has pungent digestion, and precisely because of that digestion, binds feces and urine.
Sour <s>kāñjika</s> conquers phlegm because it is sharp and hot.

children.text: kapitthaṃ tu raukṣyāt kaphaṃ pittaṃ ca śītavīryatvāt ||
children.translated_text: But <s>kapittha</s>, because of dryness, conquers phlegm, and because of cold potency, conquers bile.

children.text: āmalakaṃ pittaṃ śītavīryatvāt svādupākitayā ca kaphaṃ raukṣyāl lāghavāc ca śaityaraukṣyalāghavais tu na vātam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Āmalaka</s> conquers bile because of cold potency; because of sweet digestion it conquers phlegm, and because of dryness and lightness, and because of coldness, dryness, and lightness, it does not produce wind.

children.text: lavaṇaṃ saindhavaṃ svādupākatayā pittaṃ jayati lāghavāt kapham ||
children.translated_text: Rock salt, because of sweet digestion, conquers bile, and because of lightness, phlegm.

children.text: kaṭukāpi śuṇṭhī snehauṣṇyasvādupākatayā vātaṃ jayati pippalī ca laśuno 'pi snehauṣṇyagauravaiḥ palāṇḍuś ca ||
children.translated_text: Dry ginger, though pungent, conquers wind because of unctuousness, heat, and sweet digestion; so also long pepper and garlic, and onion because of unctuousness, heat, and heaviness.

children.text: sa tu snehagauravābhyāṃ janayati śleṣmāṇam vṛddhaṃ ca mūlakaṃ svādupākatayā ||
children.translated_text: But that onion produces phlegm because of unctuousness and heaviness; and old radish does so because of sweet digestion.
Bitter substances conquer bile.

children.text: tiktā api vyāghrīviśalyārkavāruṇya uṣṇavīryatvāt pittaṃ janayanti ||
children.translated_text: Yet bitter <s>vyāghrī</s>, <s>viśalyā</s>, <s>arka</s>, and <s>vāruṇī</s> produce bile because they have hot potency.

children.text: kaṣāyatiktaṃ mahat pañcamūlaṃ vātaṃ jayati na tu pittam uṣṇavīryatvāt ||
children.translated_text: The great five roots, astringent and bitter, conquer wind, but not bile, because they have hot potency.
And horse gram and other astringents do so also because they have sour digestion.
This has been stated only as an illustration.
Thus.
Although all are present, he states the reason for the causal efficacy of just one with 'whichever.'
By strength means by superiority of strength.

children.text: balaṃ ca dvividhaṃ kṛtrimam akṛtrimaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: And strength is twofold: artificial and natural.

children.text: mātrādhikyena sahāyasampattyā ca kṛtaṃ kṛtrimaṃ svābhāvikam akṛtrimam ||
children.translated_text: What is produced by excess of measure and abundance of auxiliaries is artificial; what is innate is natural.
There he states natural strength with 'taste.'
Those two are taste and digestion.
Those are digestion and potency.
'Removes' means conquers.

children.text: balasāmye kṛtrimabalatulyatve yatra rasavipākayostulyamātratvaṃ tulyasahāyatvaṃ ca tatra rasādvipāko balī mātrāsahāyavaiṣamye tu yo mātrādhikaḥ sahāyādhiko vā sa balīty arthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When strength is equal, that is, when artificial strength is equal, where taste and digestion have equal measure and equal auxiliaries, digestion is stronger than taste; but when measure and auxiliaries are unequal, whichever has greater measure or greater auxiliaries is stronger. This is the meaning.
The same should be said also with regard to potency and the rest.
But in the Saṃgraha it is said:
Even when mutually opposed, taste and the others, in accomplishing an effect,

children.text: nāvaśyaṃ syur vighātāya guṇadoṣā mitho yathā ||
children.translated_text: do not necessarily obstruct one another, just as qualities and faults do not necessarily do so mutually.
Taste, potency, and the rest, because of the increase and decrease of the elements,
reside in a substance as of one form or of two forms.
Sweetness, coldness, sliminess, unctuousness, heaviness, and dullness,

children.text: saha vṛttyā sthitāḥ kṣīre na tv ānūpaudakāmiṣe ||
children.translated_text: exist together in milk, but not in the meat of marsh and aquatic animals.

children.text: guṇā dravyeṣu ye coktāsta eva tanudoṣayoḥ
children.translated_text: The qualities that are stated in substances are the very same in the body and in the <s>doṣas</s>;
therefore their maintenance, increase, and decrease have substances as their causes.
One should know the taste by contact and by keeping it in the mouth;
one should know the potency and digestion of substances from the completion of their action.
In ghee, oil, molasses, and the like, which are listed in the sweet group,
the sixfold taste does not apply by distinctions such as qualities and flavor.
Let there be innumerability because of difference, or unity because of the characteristic of flavor;
but the difference that is imagined in slight measure because of the increase and decrease of the elements,
because it is mixed and because its effect is equivalent, is not intended to be expressed.
Even when there is difference among heaviness and the other qualities, this does not transgress its own class.

children.text: saṃkhyābhedo yathā nāsti rasānāmapi sa kramaḥ
children.translated_text: Just as there is no difference in number, so too that sequence does not apply to tastes.
For coating of the mouth and the like is seen in all substances such as ghee and so on.

children.text: na ca taddāḍimādyeṣu ṣaḍevāto rasāḥ smṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: And that is not found in pomegranate and the like; therefore the tastes are remembered as only six.
And if there were infinity or unity, there would be no systematic treatment of varied objects.
The heavy and the like are called potency when they possess power; otherwise they are qualities.
Because they lack sharp efficacy, those twelve qualities are merely qualities.
Thus.
Now, prabhāva.
He defines <s>prabhāva</s> (special efficacy) with 'when taste and the rest are the same.'

children.text: dvayor dravyayo rasādisāmye saty apyekasya yadviśiṣṭaṃ karma dṛśyate tat prabhāvajam ||
children.translated_text: When two substances are alike in taste and the rest, yet a distinctive action is seen in one of them, that is born from <s>prabhāva</s>.

children.text: tatra yo dravyadharmo hetuḥ sa prabhāva ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that the property of the substance which is the cause in that case is <s>prabhāva</s>.
He gives an example of <s>prabhāva</s> with '<s>dantī</s>'.

children.text: rasādaya uktāś carakeṇa kaṭukaḥ kaṭukaḥ pāke vīryoṣṇaś citrako mataḥ
children.translated_text: The tastes and so forth were stated by <s>Caraka</s>: <s>citraka</s> is held to be pungent, pungent in digestion, and hot in potency.

children.text: tadvaddantī prabhāvāt tu virecayati sā naram ||
children.translated_text: Like it, <s>dantī</s>, however, purges a person by <s>prabhāva</s>.
Thus.

children.text: madhukamṛdvīkayoḥ kṣīraghṛtayośca madhurarasapākatvena śītavīryatvena ca sāmye'pi mṛdvīkaiva virecanī na madhukam ghṛtameva dīpanaṃ na kṣīram ||
children.translated_text: Although <s>madhuka</s> and grapes, and milk and ghee, are alike in having sweet taste and post-digestive effect and in having cold potency, only the grape is purgative, not <s>madhuka</s>; only ghee kindles digestion, not milk.
In the compendium, however, another example is also given.
Garlic, through pungent digestion and taste, unctuousness, and heaviness, conquers phlegm and wind.

children.text: laśuno vātakaphakṛnna tu tair eva yadguṇaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Yet by those very qualities it does not produce wind and phlegm.

children.text: mitho viruddhān vātādīn lohitādyā jayanti yat
children.translated_text: That <s>lohita</s> and the others conquer wind and the other humors that are mutually opposed,
and that <s>yavaka</s> and the others produce them: this is the manifestation of <s>prabhāva</s>.
That <s>śirīṣa</s> and the like destroy poison, while sleep and the like increase it,
and the various kinds of action belonging to gems, mantras, and medicines,
such as drawing out a dart, producing male offspring, protection, weapon control, and the like,
and that an antidote restrains poison even by sight and so forth,
that something purges, that an aphrodisiac quickly produces semen,
and that a substance acts upward or downward, or is pacifying and the like,
and whatever further matter, depending on dosage and the rest, has been described at length,
all that is born from <s>prabhāva</s>; therefore it is called inconceivable.

children.text: rasena vīryeṇa guṇaiśca karma dravyaṃ vipākena ca yad vidadhyāt
children.translated_text: Whatever action a substance would perform through taste, potency, qualities, and post-digestive effect,

children.text: sadyo'nyathā tat kurute prabhāvāddhetor atas tasya na gocaro 'sti ||
children.translated_text: it immediately does otherwise through <s>prabhāva</s>; therefore its cause is not within ordinary reach.
Thus.
He sums up the meaning of the chapter with 'generally.'
Of substance and the others down to <s>prabhāva</s>.
He again states an exception to the action described in general terms with 'and that.'

children.text: tat sāmānyoktaṃ karma bhidyate viśiṣyate anyathākriyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: That action stated in general is divided, specified, or made otherwise; this is the meaning.

children.text: kena vicitrapratyayārabdhadravyabhedena vicitrāḥ parasparavilakṣaṇāḥ pratyayāḥ kāraṇabhūtā mahābhūtasaṃghātāḥ tair ārabdhaṃ yad dravyaṃ tasya bhedo dravyāntaraviśiṣṭatvaṃ tena ||
children.translated_text: By what? By the difference of a substance produced from varied causal factors: varied means mutually distinct; the causal factors are aggregates of the great elements, and the difference of the substance produced by them is its being distinguished from another substance.
Since the common and particular difference extending from the earthy substance to barley was stated earlier, he says 'again that.'

children.text: etaduktaṃ bhavati kvaciddravye yādṛgeva bhūtasaṃghāto dravyasyārambhakaḥ tādṛgeva rasādīnām ||
children.translated_text: What is being said is this: in some substance, just the same aggregate of elements that originates the substance also originates its taste and the rest.
What is produced from the same causal factors does not go beyond those common qualities.

children.text: kvacidanyādṛgbhūtasaṃghāto dravyasyārambhako 'nyādṛg rasasyānyādṛk guṇasyetyādi tadvicitrapratyayārabdham tatsāmānyaguṇān atikrāmati ||
children.translated_text: But in some case the aggregate of elements originating the substance is of one kind, that of the taste is of another, that of the quality is of another, and so on; what is produced from such varied causal factors goes beyond those common qualities.
For that purpose begins the discussion of 'from liquid substances' and 'known by their own nature' and so on.
He gives examples of difference among substances with 'sweet.'

children.text: yavagodhū mayormatsyapayasoḥ siṃhaśūkarayośca svādutvagurutvābhyāṃ tulyatve 'pi yavamatsyasiṃhānāṃ vicitrapratyayārabdhatvāt vātalaprabhāvatvoṣṇavīryatvakaṭuvipākitvāni svādutvagurutvaviparī śodhanādidravyagaṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although barley and wheat, fish and milk, and lion and boar are alike in sweetness and heaviness, because barley, fish, and lion are produced from varied causal factors, their wind-producing <s>prabhāva</s>, hot potency, pungent post-digestive effect, and the groups of purifying and other drugs are contrary to sweetness and heaviness.
Among these, he states the emetic group with '<s>madana</s>, <s>madhuka</s>,' and so on.
<s>Madana</s> is <s>gela</s>.
<s>Madhuka</s> is licorice.
<s>Lambā</s> is bitter gourd.
<s>Nimba</s> is <s>picumanda</s>.
<s>Bimbī</s> is <s>kaṭutuṇḍikerī</s>.
<s>Viśālā</s> is <s>indravāruṇī</s>.
<s>Trapusa</s> is bitter cucumber.
<s>Kuṭaja</s> is <s>vatsaka</s>.
<s>Mūrvā</s> is <s>madhurasā</s>.
<s>Devadālī</s> is <s>jīmūtaka</s>.
<s>Kṛmighna</s> is <s>viḍaṅga</s>.
<s>Vidula</s> is reed.
<s>Dahana</s> is <s>citraka</s>.
<s>Citrā</s> is <s>citrāṇḍikā</s>, and the pungent fruit and leaf of pointed gourd.
The two <s>kośavatī</s>s are bitter <s>kośātakī</s> and royal <s>kośātakī</s>.
<s>Karañja</s> is <s>naktamāla</s>.
<s>Kaṇā</s> is long pepper.
The salt is rock salt.
<s>Vacā</s> is <s>ugrā</s>.
<s>Elā</s> is <s>truṭi</s>.
<s>Sarṣapa</s> is <s>rakṣoghna</s>.
'Emetics' means agents of vomiting.
The plural is for the sake of indicating a plurality of qualities.

children.text: tena vamanādidravyāṇāṃ yasya kasyacit trikacatuṣkapañcakādeḥ prayojakatvam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, among emetic and similar substances, any group of three, four, five, or the like may serve as the operative set.

children.text: uktaṃ ca suśrutena samastaṃ vargamardhaṃ vā yathālābhamathāpi vā ||
children.translated_text: And this was said by <s>Suśruta</s>: the wise physician should employ the whole class,
or half of it, or even whatever is available, in the actions for which they have been prescribed.
Thus.
And this is an indicative statement.
For that very reason the author of the compendium studies more: the fruits, flowers, and leaves of <s>madana</s>, <s>jīmūta</s>, <s>ikṣvāku</s>, and the two <s>kośātakī</s>s,

and the autumnal fruits of <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>karañja</s>, <s>trapusa</s>, <s>sarṣapa</s>, <s>pippalī</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, <s>elā</s>, <s>pratyakpuṣpī</s>, <s>hareṇu</s>, <s>pṛthvīkā</s>, <s>kustumbari</s>, and <s>prapunnaṭa</s>, and of <s>hastiparṇī</s>.

The roots of <s>kovidāra</s>, <s>karbudāra</s>, <s>ariṣṭa</s>, <s>aśvagandhā</s>, <s>nīpa</s>, <s>vidula</s>, <s>bimbī</s>, <s>bandhujīvaka</s>, white <s>śaṇapuṣpī</s>, <s>sadāpuṣpā</s>, <s>vacā</s>, <s>citrā</s>, <s>citraka</s>, <s>mṛgairvāru</s>, <s>kendravāruṇī</s>, <s>suṣavī</s>, <s>caturaṅgula</s>, <s>svādukaṇṭaka</s>, <s>pāṭhā</s>, <s>pāṭalī</s>, <s>śārṅgeṣṭā</s>, <s>madhuka</s>, <s>mūrvā</s>, <s>saptaparṇa</s>, <s>somavalka</s>, <s>dvīpi</s>, <s>śigru</s>, <s>sumanas</s>, <s>saumanasyā</s>, <s>yavānī</s>, <s>vṛścīvā</s>, <s>punarnavā</s>, the great <s>sahā</s>, the small <s>sahā</s>, sugarcane stalk, <s>kaṭaka</s>, long-pepper root, <s>cavikā</s>, <s>nalada</s>, <s>uśīra</s>, and <s>hrīvera</s>.

The piths of <s>śālmalī</s>, <s>śālmalukā</s>, <s>bhadraparṇī</s>, <s>airāvaṇī</s>, <s>upodakā</s>, <s>uddālaka</s>, <s>dhanvana</s>, <s>rasāñjana</s>, <s>rājādana</s>, <s>upacitrā</s>, <s>gopaśṛṅgāṭikā</s>, and <s>picchā</s>.
The flower of <s>priyaṅgu</s>.
The leaf of <s>tālīsa</s>.
The tubers of turmeric and ginger.
The heartwoods of <s>madhūka</s> and tree-turmeric.
And <s>tagara</s>, <s>guḍūcī</s>, honey, treacle, milk, alkalis, and salts: these are useful for emesis.
Thus.
He states the purgative group with '<s>nikumbha</s>, <s>kumbha</s>,' and so on.
<s>Nikumbha</s> is <s>dantī</s>.
<s>Kumbha</s> is <s>trivṛt</s>.
<s>Triphalā</s> is well known.
<s>Gavākṣī</s> is white-flowered <s>indravāruṇī</s>.
<s>Snuk</s> is <s>snuhī</s>.
<s>Śaṅkhinī</s> resembles black collyrium and has white flowers.
<s>Nīlinī</s> is <s>kālāñjanikā</s>.
<s>Tilvaka</s> is <s>rodhra</s>.
<s>Śamyāka</s> is <s>āragvadha</s>.
<s>Kampilla</s> is <s>raktāṅga</s>.
<s>Hemadugdhā</s> is <s>hemāvatī</s>, of the nature of <s>kaṅkuṣṭha</s>.

But in the compendium more is stated: the roots of <s>trivṛt</s>, <s>śyāmā</s>, <s>dantī</s>, <s>dravantī</s>, <s>śaṅkhinī</s>, <s>saptalā</s>, <s>ajagandhā</s>, <s>ajaśṛṅgī</s>, <s>vacā</s>, <s>gavākṣī</s>, <s>chagalāntrī</s>, <s>suvarṇakṣīrī</s>, <s>citraka</s>, <s>kiṇihī</s>, the lesser five roots, <s>vṛścīvā</s>, <s>punarnavā</s>, <s>palaṅkaṣā</s>, <s>vāstuka</s>, vegetable greens, and <s>sāla</s> roots,
the barks of <s>tilvaka</s>, <s>ramyaka</s>, <s>kampilla</s>, and <s>pāṭalī</s>,

the fruits of <s>triphalā</s>, <s>pīlu</s>, <s>priyāla</s>, <s>bakula</s>, <s>badara</s>, <s>karkandhu</s>, <s>kāśmarya</s>, <s>parūṣaka</s>, grapes, <s>nīlinī</s>, <s>klītana</s>, <s>kakṣīraka</s>, <s>udakīryā</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, areca nut, and <s>pañcāṅgula</s>, and the fruits and leaves of <s>caturaṅgula</s>,
the bark, fruits, and leaves of <s>pūtīka</s>,
the milky exudations of <s>mahāvṛkṣa</s>, <s>saptaparṇa</s>, and <s>jyotiṣmatī</s>,
and milk, whey, liquor, fermented grain-gruel, and urines: these are useful for purgation.
<s>Kośātakī</s>, <s>devadālī</s>, <s>saptalā</s>, <s>kāravellikā</s> juice, latex of <s>arka</s>, and hot water have both characters.
Thus.
He states the decoction-enema group with '<s>madana</s>' and so on.
<s>Kuṣṭha</s> is <s>pākala</s>.
<s>Daśamūla</s> consists of the great and the small five roots.
<s>Dāru</s> is <s>devadāru</s>.
<s>Rāsnā</s> is well known.
Barley has sharp awns.
<s>Miśi</s> is <s>śatapuṣpā</s>.
<s>Kṛtavedhana</s> is pungent <s>kośātakī</s>.
<s>Kulattha</s> is a particular kind of leguminous grain.
Honey is bee-honey.
But in the compendium more is stated.

children.text: vastiṣu tu teṣu teṣv avasthāntareṣu yānyupayujyante dravyāṇi tāny asaṃkhyeyatvān nopadiśyante ||
children.translated_text: Among those various enemas, the substances used in one or another condition are not taught, because they are innumerable.

children.text: rasaskandhebhya eva yathādoṣaṃ yathāvasthaṃ ca vibhajet ||
children.translated_text: One should classify them from the groups of tastes themselves, according to the doṣa and according to the condition.

In all of them, generally, there are the fruits of <s>madana</s>, <s>kuṭaja</s>, <s>jīmūtaka</s>, <s>ikṣvāku</s>, the two <s>kośātakī</s>s, cucumber, white mustard, and <s>śatāhvā</s>; the roots of <s>balā</s>, <s>daśamūla</s>, castor, <s>trivṛt</s>, <s>vacā</s>, <s>yaṣṭyāhva</s>, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>rāsnā</s>, <s>punarnavā</s>, and <s>kaṭtṛṇa</s>; and <s>sarala</s>, <s>devadāru</s>, <s>hapuṣā</s>, asafoetida, <s>rasāñjana</s>, the three pungents, leaves, cardamom, <s>mṛtā</s>, barley, jujube, horse gram, jaggery, salt, whey, fermented grain-gruel, urine, fats, milk, and honey.
Thus.
He states the nasal-medication group with '<s>vellā</s>, <s>apāmārga</s>,' and so on.
<s>Surālā</s> is the best resin of <s>sarja</s>.
The seeds of <s>śirīṣa</s>, <s>bṛhatī</s>, and <s>śigru</s>.
The heartwood of <s>madhuka</s>.
<s>Tārkṣyaśaila</s> is <s>rasāñjana</s>.
The two <s>truṭi</s>s are the two cardamoms.
<s>Pṛthvīkā</s> is <s>bāṣpikā</s>.

But in the compendium more is stated: the fruits of <s>apāmārga</s>, <s>viḍaṅga</s>, black pepper, long pepper, <s>śirīṣa</s>, <s>bilva</s>, goat-related substances, <s>ajamodā</s>, eggplant, <s>pṛthvīkā</s>, cardamom, and <s>hareṇu</s>.
The leaves of <s>tālīśa</s>, <s>tamāla</s>, <s>tarkārī</s>, and the <s>harītaka</s> group.
The fruits and leaves of mustard.
The fruits, leaves, and bark of <s>śigru</s>.
The tubers and leaves of turmeric, radish, garlic, and dry ginger.
The tubers of <s>ativiṣā</s>.

The roots of <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>vacā</s>, <s>bhārṅgī</s>, white <s>kiṇihī</s>, <s>nāgadantī</s>, <s>jyotiṣmatī</s>, <s>gavākṣī</s>, <s>vayaḥsthā</s>, <s>vṛścikālī</s>, <s>bimbī</s>, and <s>karañja</s>.
The flowers and roots of <s>arka</s> and <s>alarka</s>.
The seeds of <s>rodhra</s>, <s>madana</s>, <s>saptaparṇa</s>, <s>bimba</s>, and <s>pīlu</s>.
The flowers of <s>muraṅgī</s>, citron, and clove.
The exudations of <s>aguru</s>, <s>suradāru</s>, <s>sarala</s>, <s>śallakī</s>, <s>jiṅgiṇī</s>, <s>aśana</s>, <s>rasāñjana</s>, and <s>hiṅgula</s>.
The heartwoods of <s>śāla</s>, palm, <s>madhūka</s>, and <s>dārvī</s>.
The barks of <s>tejasvinī</s>, <s>meṣaśṛṅgī</s>, <s>varāṅga</s>, <s>iṅgudī</s>, and the two <s>bṛhatī</s>s.
The pith of <s>rājādana</s>.
Honey, salts, liquors, and the dung, urine, and bile of cattle and the like: other such substances too are pacifiers of the senses.

children.text: tathā snehāḥ kṣāraṃ raktaṃ māṃsaraso dhānyarasastoyamiti śirovirecanopayogīni ||
children.translated_text: Likewise fats, alkali, blood, meat-broth, grain-liquor, and water: these are useful for purgation of the head.

<s>Madhuka</s>, lotus stalk, <s>mañjiṣṭhā</s>, <s>sārivā</s>, <s>mustā</s>, <s>punnāga</s>, <s>nāgakeśara</s>, cardamom, <s>vālukā</s>, <s>suvarṇatvak</s>, tamāla leaves, <s>pṛthvīkā</s>, <s>hareṇu</s>, lac, <s>śatapuṣpā</s>, <s>śallakī</s>, sugar, <s>damanaka</s>, <s>marubaka</s>, banyan, <s>udumbara</s>, holy fig, <s>plakṣa</s>, <s>rodhra</s> bark, lotus and blue lotus, and all fragrant substances except <s>kuṣṭha</s> and <s>tagara</s> are generally useful for practical fumigation.

<s>Aguru</s>, <s>guggulu</s>, <s>śallaka</s>, <s>śileyaka</s>, <s>nalada</s>, <s>hrīvera</s>, <s>hareṇu</s>, <s>uśīra</s>, <s>musta</s>, <s>dhyāmaka</s>, <s>varāṅga</s>, <s>śrīveṣṭaka</s>, <s>sthauṇeyaka</s>, <s>paripelava</s>, <s>elavāluka</s>, <s>kanduruka</s>, <s>sarjarasa</s>, <s>yaṣṭyāhva</s>, fruit-pith, oily matter, beeswax, the marrow of <s>bilva</s> fruit, sesame, barley, black gram, and saffron, as well as fat, marrow, muscle-fat, and ghee, are used for oleating smoke.

children.text: śirovirekadravyāṇi gandhadravyāṇi ca tīkṣṇāni manohvā haritālaṃ ceti tīkṣṇadhūmopayogīni ||
children.translated_text: The substances for evacuating the head, fragrant substances, and sharp substances, together with <s>manohvā</s> and orpiment, are used for sharp smoke.
Thus.
He states the vāta-destroying group with the words '<s>bhadradāru</s>, <s>nata</s>,' and so on.
<s>Bhadradāru</s> is <s>devadāru</s>.
<s>Nata</s> is <s>tagara</s>.
The <s>vīratarādi</s> and <s>vidāryādi</s> groups are two groups that will be stated below.
Among them, those that are repeated are to be added in double quantity.

children.text: saṃgrahe tu bhadradārukuṣṭhatagaravaruṇabalātibalārtagalakacchurābāhlīkakuberākṣivatsādanyarkālarkakiṃśukakatakabhārṅgīkārpāsīvṛścikālīpattūraprabhṛtīni vidāryādir vakṣyamāṇagaṇo vīratarādis tṛṇākhyavarjyāni ṣaṭ pañcamūlāni ceti vātaśamanāni ||
children.translated_text: But in the Compendium, <s>bhadradāru</s>, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>tagara</s>, <s>varuṇa</s>, <s>balā</s>, <s>atibalā</s>, <s>ārtagala</s>, <s>kacchurā</s>, <s>bāhlīka</s>, <s>kuberākṣi</s>, <s>vatsādani</s>, <s>arka</s>, <s>alarka</s>, <s>kiṃśuka</s>, <s>kataka</s>, <s>bhārṅgī</s>, <s>kārpāsī</s>, <s>vṛścikālī</s>, <s>pattūra</s>, and the like; the <s>vidāryādi</s> group to be stated below; the <s>vīratarādi</s> group; and the six sets of five roots except those called grasses, are said to pacify vāta.
Thus.
He states the pitta-destroying group with '<s>dūrvā</s>,' and so on.
<s>Anantā</s> is <s>durālabhā</s>.
<s>Gundrā</s> is <s>erakā</s>.
<s>Śītapākī</s> is <s>guñjā</s>.
The two steady ones are <s>śāliparṇī</s> and <s>pṛśniparṇī</s>.
<s>Vanya</s> is small <s>musta</s>.
The <s>nyagrodhādi</s>, <s>padmakādi</s>, and <s>sārivādi</s> groups are groups that will be stated below.
Here too, repeated items are to be doubled.

But in the Compendium, <s>dūrvā</s>, <s>anantā</s>, <s>mocarasa</s>, <s>mañjiṣṭhā</s>, <s>paripelava</s>, <s>kālā</s>, <s>kālīyaka</s>, <s>kadalī</s>, <s>kandalī</s>, <s>payasyā</s>, <s>ātmaguptā</s>, coconut, date, grape, <s>vidārī</s>, jujube, <s>balā</s>, <s>nāgabalā</s>, <s>nāgapuṣpā</s>, <s>śatāvarī</s>, <s>śītapākī</s>, <s>odanapākī</s>, <s>tṛṇaśūlī</s>, the two <s>aṃśumatī</s>s, <s>ariṣṭaka</s>, <s>aṭarūṣaka</s>, <s>ketaka</s>, <s>priyaṅgu</s>, <s>dhātakī</s>, <s>dhava</s>, <s>dhanvana</s>, <s>syandana</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>kadara</s>, <s>priyāla</s>, palm, <s>śāla</s>, <s>sarja</s>, <s>tiniśa</s>, <s>aśvakarṇa</s>, <s>gundrā</s>, <s>vānīra</s>, lotus, <s>padmaka</s>, lotus seed, lotus stalk, water-lily, blue lotus, fragrant lotus, white lotus, hundred-petalled lotus, <s>śevāla</s>, <s>kahlāra</s>, <s>utpala</s>, <s>kākolī</s>, <s>utpalikā</s>, <s>śālūka</s>, <s>śṛṅgāṭaka</s>, <s>kaseruka</s>, <s>krauñcādana</s>, and the like are of cooling potency.

children.text: sārivādiḥ padmakādiḥ paṭolādirnyagrodhādirdāhaharo mahākaṣāyas tṛṇapañcamūlaṃ ceti pittaśamanāni ||
children.translated_text: The <s>sārivādi</s>, <s>padmakādi</s>, <s>paṭolādi</s>, and <s>nyagrodhādi</s> groups, the great decoction that removes burning, and the five grass roots are said to pacify pitta.
Thus.
He states the śleṣman-destroying group with '<s>āragvadhādi</s>'.
These are the seven groups that will be stated below.
Here too, repeated items are to be doubled.

children.text: saṃgrahe tu śītaśivaśatapuṣpāsaralasuradārurāsneṅgudīsātalāsumanaḥkākādanīlāṅgalikāhastikarṇamuñjātalāmajjakaprabhṛtīny āragvadhādir asanādir arkādiḥ surasādir muṣkakādir vatsakādir mustādiḥ śītaghno mahākaṣāyo vallīkaṇṭakapañcamūle ceti śleṣmapraśamanānīti ||
children.translated_text: But in the Compendium, <s>śīta</s>, <s>śiva</s>, <s>śatapuṣpā</s>, <s>sarala</s>, <s>suradāru</s>, <s>rāsnā</s>, <s>iṅgudī</s>, <s>sātalā</s>, <s>sumanas</s>, <s>kākādanī</s>, <s>lāṅgalikā</s>, <s>hastikarṇa</s>, <s>muñjātala</s>, <s>majjaka</s>, and the like; the <s>āragvadhādi</s>, <s>asanādi</s>, <s>arkādi</s>, <s>surasādi</s>, <s>muṣkakādi</s>, <s>vatsakādi</s>, and <s>mustādi</s> groups; the heat-removing great decoction; and the five roots of creepers and thorny plants are said to pacify śleṣman.
Thus.
Now the great decoctions.
Among them, he states the life-promoting group with '<s>jīvantī</s>,' and so on.

children.text: saṃgrahe tu ānantyādau ṣadhānāmāmayānāṃ cānantā eva kaṣāyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But in the Compendium, because diseases are endless and so on, the decoctions too are endless.

children.text: ye tu sutarāmupayogavantaḥ prakarṣavartino vā te jīvanīyādisaṃjñāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those, however, that are especially useful or are prominent are designated by names such as life-promoting.
Each is a combination of ten decoction-substances.
This is precisely for the understanding of people of dull intellect.
For intelligent people, however, it is only for showing examples.

children.text: śakyaṃ hi buddhimadbhiḥ svādusnigdhaśītādīn jīvantyādiṣu sādhāraṇān guṇānālocya kṣīrekṣukṣaudradrākṣākṣoḍavidarikandadiṣvapi tadguṇeṣu jīvanīyāditvam avadhārayitum ||
children.translated_text: For intelligent people, after considering the common qualities such as sweetness, unctuousness, and coolness in <s>jīvantī</s> and the others, can determine the life-promoting character and the like also in milk, sugarcane, honey, grapes, walnuts, <s>vidārī</s> tubers, and other things possessing those qualities.
For a person of dull intellect, following exactly what has been stated is best.

children.text: vyastāśca te catvāri śatāni pañcāśadadhikāni tadabhidhānānyeva ||
children.translated_text: And when separated out, they are four hundred and fifty, bearing those very names.

children.text: yadyapi ca tāni tānyeva dravyāṇīti dravyasaṅkaraḥ kaṣāyeṣu tathā'pi na saṃjñāvirodhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although there is mixture of substances among the decoctions, since the same substances recur, still there is no conflict of designations.
For even a single substance can accomplish many actions.

children.text: tatra lavaṇavarjyāḥ pañca rasāḥ kalpanāyāṃ kaṣāyā ityucyante tadyonitvāt ||
children.translated_text: There, in preparation, the five tastes except salt are called decoctions, because they are their source.

children.text: lavaṇe tu niryāsādikalpanānām asambhavaḥ pṛthagupayogopakārarahitatvāc ca nairarthakyamiti ||
children.translated_text: But in the case of salt, since preparations such as extracts are impossible and since it lacks assistance for separate use, it would be pointless.
And here there are verses.

children.text: jīvantī kākolyau dve mede mudgamāṣaparṇyau ca
children.translated_text: <s>Jīvantī</s>, the two <s>kākolī</s>s, the two <s>medā</s>s, and <s>mudgaparṇī</s> and <s>māṣaparṇī</s>,
together with <s>ṛṣabhaka</s>, <s>jīvaka</s>, and <s>madhuka</s>: this is the group called life-promoting.
<s>Vāṭyā</s>, <s>balā</s>, <s>payasyā</s>, the two <s>kākolī</s>s, <s>ṛṣabha</s>, and <s>vājigandhā</s>,
<s>kṣīriṇī</s>, <s>rājakṣavaka</s>, and <s>bhāradvājī</s>: this is the nourishing group.
<s>Vāṭyā</s> is <s>atibalā</s>.
<s>Payasyā</s> is <s>ṛṣyagandhā</s>, or <s>vidārī</s>, or <s>kṣīravidārī</s>.
<s>Kṣīriṇī</s> is <s>śrīparṇī</s>.
<s>Rājakṣavaka</s> is <s>dugdhikā</s>.
<s>Bhāradvājī</s> is wild cotton.

children.text: haimavatī ciribilvaṃ mustā kuṣṭhaṃ vacā haridre ca
children.translated_text: <s>Haimavatī</s>, <s>ciribilva</s>, <s>mustā</s>, <s>kuṣṭha</s>, <s>vacā</s>, and the two <s>haridrā</s>s,
<s>citraka</s>, <s>kaṭukā</s>, and <s>ativiṣā</s>: this class is called scraping.
<s>Haimavatī</s> is white <s>vacā</s>.
<s>Arka</s>, <s>eraṇḍa</s>, <s>citrā</s>, <s>citraka</s>, <s>ciribilva</s>, <s>śaṅkhinī</s>, and <s>saralā</s>,
<s>hemakṣīrī</s>, <s>kaṭukā</s>, and <s>vahnimukhī</s> are the purgative substances.
<s>Citrā</s> is <s>dantī</s>.
<s>Saralā</s> is <s>trivṛt</s>.
<s>Vahnimukhī</s> is <s>lāṅgalī</s>.
Honey, <s>madhuka</s>, <s>pṛśniparṇī</s>, the fruit of <s>kadā</s>, <s>rodhra</s>, <s>priyaṅgu</s>, and <s>takya</s>,
<s>ambaṣṭhakī</s>, <s>samaṅgā</s>, and <s>mocarasa</s>: these are the healing group.
<s>Ambaṣṭhakī</s> is <s>mācikā</s>.
Because of the combination of <s>hiṅgu</s>, pepper, sour <s>vetasa</s>, <s>dīpyaka</s>, and the kernel of <s>bhallātaka</s>,
this group, together with the five <s>kolas</s>, is prescribed as a stimulant of digestion.
<s>Aindratirasā</s>, <s>payasyā</s>, that which is taught by the sages, <s>sthirā</s>, <s>balā</s>, and <s>atibalā</s>,

children.text: iti balyo daśako'yaṃ hayagandhā rohiṇī ṛṣabhī ||
children.translated_text: this set of ten strengthening drugs is thus stated, with <s>hayagandhā</s>, <s>rohiṇī</s>, and <s>ṛṣabhī</s>.
<s>Aindrī</s> means <s>indravāruṇī</s>.

children.text: atirasā snehavidhim adhyāyaṃ vyākhyātuṃ pratijānīte atheti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Atirasā</s>: with the word 'now' he promises to explain the chapter on the procedure for oleation.
For in the preceding chapter the medicines were stated.
Their application must now be described.
And that is manifold, divided into oleation, sudation, purificatory therapy, evacuative enemas, nasal therapy, fumigation, gargles, eye drops, eye-nourishing applications, and so on.

children.text: cikitsākalikāyāṃ tu prāk pācanaṃ snehavidhis tataś ca svedas tataḥ syād vamanaṃ virekaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But in the <s>Cikitsākalikā</s>: first comes digestion of immature matter, then the oleation procedure, then sudation, then emesis and purgation should follow;
decoction-enema and oil-enema treatment, nasal therapy, and the sequence: such is the order of the best physicians.
At the beginning, with decoctions of <s>rāsnā</s>, pointed gourd, <s>picumanda</s>, and milk, or with waters of dry ginger, <s>aṭarūṣaka</s>, and the three fruits,

children.text: pakvāmadoṣavapuṣas tadanantaraṃ hi sneho hitaḥ surabhivāsakakaṭphalādiḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: once the body's doṣas have been ripened from the unripe state, then oleation is indeed beneficial, with fragrant <s>vāsaka</s>, <s>kaṭphala</s>, and the like. Thus.

children.text: rāsnākvāthāditrayaṃ śuṇṭhīkvāthāditrayaṃ vā vātāditraye kramāt pācanam ||
children.translated_text: The three beginning with a decoction of <s>rāsnā</s>, or the three beginning with a decoction of dry ginger, are digestives respectively for the triad beginning with <s>vāta</s>.
Among these, oleation is treated in this chapter.
For this very reason this is the procedure of oleation.
There he states the oleating substance with the phrase 'heavy and cold.'
He states the drying substance as the opposite.
Because drying is a preliminary limb of oleation, the opposite is what has qualities such as lightness.
He states the best oleating substance with the word 'ghee.'
He states the supreme oleating substance with the words 'even among these.'

children.text: saṃskārasyānuvartanāt yathā śītaiḥ saṃskṛtaṃ śītatām uṣṇaiḥ saṃskṛtam uṣṇatāṃ bhajate ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Because it follows the processing: just as something processed with cold substances takes on coldness, and something processed with hot substances takes on heat, and so on.

children.text: saṃgrahe tu mādhuryād avidāhitvāj janmādyeva ca śīlanāt ||
children.translated_text: But in the Compendium: because of its sweetness, because it does not cause burning, and because it is habituated from birth onward,
thus.

children.text: sarpirādīnāṃ snehaprayoge doṣaviśeṣeṇa tāratamyam āha pittaghnā iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the gradation of ghee and the others in the use of oleating substances according to the particular doṣa, with the words 'they pacify pitta.'

children.text: tailād vasā tato majjā tataḥ sarpiḥ pittaghnam ||
children.translated_text: From oil, fat, then marrow, and then ghee, each is more pitta-pacifying.

children.text: sarpiṣo majjā tato vasā tatas tailaṃ vātaghnaṃ kaphaghnaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: From ghee, marrow, then fat, and then oil, each is more vāta-pacifying and kapha-pacifying.
Even in a pitta disease treatable by oleation, pitta-pacifying power is stated in order to permit the use of oil.
So too elsewhere.

children.text: sarpirādīnāṃ gurutve tāratamyam āha ghṛtād iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the gradation in heaviness of ghee and the rest with the words 'from ghee.'

children.text: idānīṃ yamakaḥ snehas trivṛtaḥ sneho mahāsneha iti ca tatrocyante tatra na ca te jñāyanta ity āha ||
children.translated_text: Now, since the terms double oleation, triple oleation, and great oleation are used there, but those are not understood, he explains.
He states the three designations beginning with <s>yamaka</s> with the word 'by two.'
By those, in the order stated for heaviness.

children.text: tena ghṛtatailābhyāṃ yamakaḥ ghṛtatailavasābhis trivṛtaḥ sarvair mahān ||
children.translated_text: Thus, with ghee and oil there is double oleation; with ghee, oil, and fat there is triple oleation; with all of them there is the great one.

children.text: saṅgrahe tu snehāśayā dadhi kṣīraṃ māṃsāsthiphaladāru ca iti ||
children.translated_text: But in the Compendium: curd, milk, meat, bone, fruit, and wood are seats of oleaginous substance. Thus.
He states those who should be oleated with the words 'one to be sudated' and so on.
One to be sudated means one for whom sudation is to be performed.
One to be purified means one for whom purification is to be performed.
Addicted to the three, beginning with liquor.
A thinker is one absorbed in anxiety.
<s>Syanda</s> is inflammation of the eye.
Difficult awakening means difficult opening of the eyes.
He states those not fit for oleation with the words 'but not one with excessively weak digestive fire,' and so on.
There is no contradiction between the oleatability of a weak person and the non-oleatability of an extremely weak person.
<s>Apaprasūtā</s> means a woman who has delivered improperly.

children.text: sāmprataṃ caturṇāṃ snehānāṃ madhye yo yebhyo hitaḥ taṃ darśayann āha ||
children.translated_text: Now, showing which one among the four oleating substances is beneficial for which persons, he says:
He states the sphere of ghee with the word 'there.'
By the word 'and so on' are meant fire and the other things stated among the qualities of ghee.
He states the sphere of oil with the words 'in glandular swellings' and so on.
He states the sphere of fat and marrow with the words 'wind, sun' and so on.
In those whose tissues have been depleted by the six factors beginning with wind.
One whose channels are obstructed by wind is one whose pathways are blocked by <s>māruta</s>.
The remaining two are fat and marrow.

children.text: vasāyās tv anyad api viśeṣāntaram āha ||
children.translated_text: He also states another particular distinction concerning fat.

children.text: vasāyā viṣayāntaram āha vasā tv ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states another sphere for fat with the words 'but fat' and so on.
Burned means by fire.
Struck means by a stick or the like.
One whose womb is displaced means one whose womb has fallen from its place.

children.text: idānīṃ kasmin kāle kasya snehasyopayogaḥ śasta iti ||
children.translated_text: Now: at what time is the use of which oleating substance praised?
He states the division of times for oleating substances with the words 'oil' and so on.
Oil is used in the rainy season.
At the end of the rains, in autumn, ghee is used.
In <s>Mādhava</s>, that is spring, the remaining two are used.

children.text: nanu varṣāsu tailaṃ varṣānte sarpirvasāmajjānau mādhava iti yo 'yaṃ niyamaḥ sa kiṃcid apekṣya vartate āhosvid anapekṣya ity asmin paryanuyoga idam āha ||
children.translated_text: But the rule that oil is used in the rains, ghee at the end of the rains, and fat and marrow in <s>Mādhava</s>: does it depend on something, or is it independent? In response to this question he says the following.

children.text: yo yasminn ṛtāv uktaḥ sa tasmin sādhāraṇabhāge vimale ravau nirabhre divase śastaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whichever oleating substance is prescribed in whichever season is praised then in the common portion of that season, when the sun is clear, on a cloudless day.
The common portions are in <s>Śrāvaṇa</s>, <s>Caitra</s>, and <s>Kārttika</s>.

children.text: vyādhivaśād akāle 'pi snehanaṃ kāryam ity āha tailam iti ||
children.translated_text: He states that oleation should be done even out of season because of illness, with the word 'oil.'

children.text: tvarāyāṃ ātyayike kārye śīte 'pi snehanaṃ kāryam ||
children.translated_text: In urgency, in an emergency matter, oleation should be done even in cold weather.
And that should be with oil.

children.text: sarvasya snehasyāhny upayogād rātrāv aprayogaḥ prāpta ity āha ||
children.translated_text: Since, because every oleating substance is used by day, non-use at night would follow, he says:
Even in summer, it is to be done with ghee.
And that at night.
He states the exception to daytime oleation in conditions such as pitta with the words 'at night alone.'

children.text: divārātriniyamasya tyāge doṣam āha niśy anyatheti ||
children.translated_text: He states the fault in abandoning the rule of day and night with the words 'otherwise at night.'

children.text: yeṣāṃ divā snehanam uktaṃ teṣāṃ niśi karaṇe vātakaphajā rogāḥ syuḥ ||
children.translated_text: For those for whom daytime oleation is prescribed, if it is done at night, diseases born of vāta and kapha will arise.

children.text: yeṣāṃ niśi snehanamuktaṃ teṣāṃ divā karaṇe pittarogāḥ syuḥ ||
children.translated_text: For those for whom nighttime oleation is prescribed, if it is done by day, pitta diseases will arise.
He states the mode of administering <s>sneha</s> with 'by proper method' and so on.
'One should administer' means one should give.
By combining it with foods such as edibles and the like, and also by its use in procedures such as enema.
He states the name of the methods already mentioned with 'through difference and singleness of taste.'
The <s>sneha</s> of the kind already described is called <s>vicāraṇā</s>.
And it is of sixty-four kinds.

children.text: tatra bhakṣyādyannena yukto'nnasya madhurādirasabhedais triṣaṣṭibhedatvāt triṣaṣṭidhā ||
children.translated_text: Among these, when combined with food such as edibles, because food has sixty-three varieties through differences such as sweet taste and the like, it is of sixty-three kinds.
And, because it is overpowered by the other substances with which it is combined, it has little potency.
But when used in enema and the like, because it is unmixed, it is of one kind.
And because its quantity is small, it has little potency.
Because it has little potency, even though it is of two kinds, it is called <s>vicāraṇā</s>, since its power falls within the scope of <s>vicāraṇā</s>.
He states <s>acchapeya</s> with 'as prescribed.'

children.text: yastu kevalaḥ pīyate sa udbhūtaśaktitvānna vicāraṇāsaṃjñaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But what is drunk unmixed, because its power is manifest, is not called <s>vicāraṇā</s>.
<s>Accha</s> means unmixed.
He states the superiority of <s>acchapeya</s> with 'of <s>sneha</s>.'
<s>Kalpa</s> means application.
That is <s>acchapeya</s>.
He states the three doses of <s>acchapeya</s> with 'by two' and so on.
He states the fourth dose of <s>acchapeya</s> with 'than those.'

children.text: doṣādīn vīkṣya tābhyo'pi hrasīyasīṃ yāmapariṇāminīṃ mātrāṃ parikalpayet ||
children.translated_text: Having considered the <s>doṣa</s>s and so on, one should prescribe an even smaller dose than those, one that is digested within one watch of the day.

children.text: hrasīyasīmeva prathamaṃ yojayedityāha prāgeva tu hrasīyasīmiti ||
children.translated_text: He says that the smaller dose alone should be applied first with 'but first the smaller one.'

children.text: tatra heturuktaḥ saṅgrahe ajñātakoṣṭhe hi bahuḥ kuryājjīvitasaṃśayam
children.translated_text: The reason for this is stated in the Compendium: 'For in a patient whose bowel is unknown, a large quantity may create danger to life.'
Thus.
The proper scope of the doses is also stated there itself:
There, by the weak, those of sluggish digestive fire, children, the aged, and those of delicate constitution,
and by those who have taken unsuitable food, whose bowels are empty, and who suffer from fever, diarrhea, or cough,

children.text: hrasvā peyā sukhā sā hi parihāre'nuvartate
children.translated_text: the small dose should be drunk; for it is easy, continues during the regimen,

children.text: ciraṃ ca balyā na ruje vyāpannāpi prakalpate ||
children.translated_text: is strengthening over a long time, does not cause pain, and is manageable even if it goes wrong.
By those afflicted with urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, eruptions, skin disease, or <s>vātaśoṇita</s>,
and by those with soft bowels, the medium dose is suitable for oleation, and it works easily.
It does not diminish strength, has slow displacement, and is also sufficient for purification.
By those with large bodies, strong digestive fire and strength, and the ability to endure hunger, thirst, and distress,
by those afflicted with abdominal tumor, upward movement of wind, erysipelas, or snakebite,
and by the insane and those with difficult urination, the large dose, very quickly,
when properly applied, overcomes diseases by following all the channels.
Thus.
Now, having undertaken the time, dose, and definition of the threefold <s>sneha</s>, divided into purificatory, pacifying, and nourishing, he says the following.

children.text: śodhanasyācchapeyasya kālaṃ mātrāṃ cāha hyastana iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the time and dose of purificatory <s>acchapeya</s> with 'yesterday's' and so on.
Only when the food is digested, immediately after digestion, because the state of being hungry is the time for pacification.
'For purification' means for the sake of purification.
And its being for the sake of purification is through oleation, not directly.
For precisely this reason the dative case is used here in the sense of purpose.
But pacification and nourishment, because they are themselves means, are expressed by the words 'pacification' and 'nourishment.'

children.text: svayaṃ śodhanasya tu snehasya virecanoktaiva mātrā ||
children.translated_text: For the <s>sneha</s> that is itself purificatory, the dose is just the one stated for purgation.
'Large' means the highest dose.
But in the Compendium:
In <s>vāta</s>, ghee with salt is prescribed; in <s>pitta</s>, unmixed ghee is desired.
Where <s>kapha</s> is abundant, the physician should give it combined with alkali and the three pungents.
Thus.

children.text: śamanasyācchapeyasya kālaṃ mātrāṃ cāha śamana iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the time and dose of pacifying <s>acchapeya</s> with 'pacifying.'

children.text: anannaḥ annasambandharahitaḥ yāvad eṣa jīryati tāvanna bhoktavyamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Without food' means without connection with food; the meaning is that one should not eat as long as this is being digested.

children.text: bṛṃhaṇasya kālaṃ mātrāṃ cāha bṛṃhaṇa iti ||
children.translated_text: He states the time and dose of the nourishing kind with 'nourishing.'
Mixed according to taste and according to suitability with meat soup, wine, and the like, this is called <s>vicāraṇā</s>.
'With food' means drunk at the beginning, middle, or end of the meal.
'Small' means a small dose.
He states the proper recipient of nourishing <s>sneha</s> with 'and that is beneficial.'
One who hates <s>sneha</s> is one who is repelled by oleation.
A habitual drinker is one constantly accustomed to wine.
One habitually using <s>sneha</s> is one accustomed to <s>sneha</s>.
'Comfortable' means at ease.
He says what that, when used, does.
He states the proper scope of the nourishing kind, divided as before-food, mid-meal, and so on, with 'before, middle.'
